title: Comparison Operators
description: Asking questions that produce true or false, comparing text, and the brackets cout needs.

content.value: Questions with a Yes or No Answer
Arithmetic gives a number. A **comparison** gives a `bool`: `true` or `false`, nothing else. It is how a program asks about its own values.

items.sub: greater or equal, less or equal

content.caption: Ones and zeros: `cout` prints a `bool` as 1 for true and 0 for false. The brackets are required: `<<` is worked out before `>`, so `cout << score > pass;` does not compile.

items.title: With boolalpha
items.text: From then on it prints `true` or `false`.

content.title: Numbers or words?
content.caption: Send `boolalpha` to `cout` once, and every later `bool` prints as a word.

content.question: No `boolalpha` has been used. What does `cout << (8 >= 8) << endl;` print?
content.explain: `>=` means greater than **or equal to**, and 8 equals 8, so the answer is true. Plain `cout` prints true as 1.

steps.note: From now on, bools print as words.
Two `==`: ask "is it 1?" Yes. Nothing changes.

content.title: Watch = and == at work
content.outro: Writing `=` where you meant `==` is a famous C++ bug: it often compiles anyway and silently changes your variable. Module 4 shows exactly how.

content.question: Which line checks whether `lives` is 0?
content.explain: Two equals signs ask a question. One equals sign would store 0.

parts.label: name
parts.note: A name that says what the answer means.

content.title: A comparison stored in a bool
content.caption: No brackets needed here: `=` is always worked out last. Naming the answer makes code easier to read.
Sample run: type `75` and it prints `Passed:  true` then `Perfect: false`.

content.question: What is stored in `passed`?
content.explain: 50 is not **greater** than 50, so `score > 50` is `false`. `>=` would have given `true`.

content.value: Good news: in C++, `==` on two `string` values compares the letters. That is exactly what you want when you check what somebody typed.

content.title: Case matters
content.caption: `Y` and `y` are different characters. Module 7 shows how to change the case of text.
`<` and `>` put text in dictionary order, letter by letter. The surprise: every capital letter comes before every small letter.

content.value: This only works for `string` variables. Two quoted pieces of text, as in `"apple" < "banana"`, are not `string` values yet, and comparing them gives nonsense. Put at least one side in a `string` first.
Decimals are not stored exactly, so two sums that should agree can differ in the last digit. Use `<` and `>` freely on doubles, but be careful with `==`.

content.caption: `cout` shows only 6 significant digits, which hides the truth: the real sum is 0.30000000000000004. Real programs check that the difference is tiny instead.

items.title: Compile error
items.text: Text and a number: C++ refuses to guess what this means.

items.title: Convert first
items.text: Turn the text into an `int` with `stoi`, then compare. Gives `true`.

content.question: What does this print?
content.explain: `boolalpha` makes it print a word, and the sum is not exactly 0.3, so `==` is `false`.

practice.question: Store two ages in `int` variables. Print whether the first is older, whether they are the same age, and whether they are different. Use `boolalpha` so you see words.
Ask for a password with `getline` and print whether it equals `pocketlab`.
Ask for a temperature and store two bools: whether it is above 35, and whether it is below 10. Print both with labels.

quiz.question: What does `cout << (5 > 3);` print, with no `boolalpha`?
quiz.explain: A comparison produces a `bool`, and `cout` prints a `bool` as 1 or 0 until you send it `boolalpha`.

quiz.question: What is the difference between `=` and `==`?
options: They are the same, but `==` is clearer.
`=` stores a value; `==` asks whether two values are equal.
quiz.explain: One equals sign assigns. Two equals signs compare and produce a `bool`. Mixing them up is the classic beginner bug.

quiz.question: A person typed `yes`, stored in a `string` called `answer`. What does `answer == "yes"` give?
options: true, because == compares the letters of a string
quiz.explain: In C++, `==` on a `string` compares the characters one by one. It is case sensitive, so `Yes` would give false.

quiz.question: Why does `cout << score > pass;` fail to compile?
options: `<<` is worked out before `>`, so it needs brackets: `cout << (score > pass);`
quiz.explain: Without brackets C++ sends `score` to `cout` first, then tries to compare the result with `pass`. Brackets make the comparison happen first.

quiz.question: `cout` prints `0.1 + 0.2` as 0.3. Why does `(0.1 + 0.2) == 0.3` give false?
options: You cannot use == on doubles at all.
C++ rounds all doubles to one decimal place.
The real sum is 0.30000000000000004; cout only shows 6 significant digits.
quiz.explain: Binary fractions cannot represent 0.1 exactly, so the sum is a hair away from 0.3. `cout` rounds what it shows, but `==` checks the exact value.

quiz.question: Two `string` variables are compared with `<`. Which of these comparisons is true?
quiz.explain: Text is compared letter by letter, and every capital letter comes before every small letter. So `Zebra` comes before `apple`, and `Apple` comes before `apple`.
